5.4. Energy and Weak Boundary-Value Problems🔗

Energy arguments produce solutions without explicit formulas. Green's first identity on a coordinate box already shows the mechanism: for the difference w of two C^2 solutions with the same boundary values, the identity collapses to \int|\nabla w|^2=0, and uniqueness follows without any representation formula. The weak theory keeps that argument and drops the classical regularity. On H^1_0(\Omega) the Dirichlet form \int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v is bounded, the Poincaré inequality of the Sobolev chapter makes it coercive on bounded domains, and Lax–Milgram returns a unique weak solution of -\Delta u=f for every f\in L^2(\Omega), together with an a priori estimate, continuous dependence on the load, and a characterization as the minimizer of the Dirichlet energy. For classical competitors on a bounded domain with C^1 graph boundary, the classical Dirichlet principle gives the same characterization.

The same pattern extends to variable principal coefficients, where almost-everywhere ellipticity yields the integrated coercivity, and to lower-order terms, where coercivity can fail and a Gårding inequality with a spectral shift takes its place. The modified Helmholtz problem -\Delta u+\lambda u=f with \lambda>0 works on any measurable domain: the gradient and mass terms together control the full H^1 norm without a Poincaré inequality. The shifted lower-order solver is the input of the Fredholm section, and the weak solutions built here are what the regularity section improves.

5.4.1. Green Identities and Energy Uniqueness🔗

5.4.1.1. From boundary flux to uniqueness🔗

Green's identities are the integration-by-parts formulas that connect the classical Laplacian with the Dirichlet energy. On a coordinate box they keep the boundary term completely explicit: each pair of opposite faces contributes the corresponding outward normal derivative, so no smooth-boundary integration theory is needed.

The uniqueness argument applies the first identity to the difference w=u-v. Equal Laplacians give \Delta w=0, while agreement on every face removes the boundary flux. The remaining equality says that the integral of |\nabla w|^2 vanishes. Continuity turns this integral statement into pointwise vanishing of the gradient, and convexity of the box then makes w constant.

These are classical C^2 results with pointwise face data. The weak Dirichlet problem uses the same energy idea in H^1_0, where boundary values are encoded by the Sobolev space and integration by parts is built into the variational equation.

For a coordinate box Q=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R^{m+1} with a\le b coordinatewise, globally C^1 u, and globally C^2 v,

\int_Q u\,\Delta v =-\int_Q\nabla u\cdot\nabla v +\int_{\partial Q}u\,\partial_\nu v\,dS.

The linked theorem expands the boundary term into the signed integrals over the upper and lower coordinate faces.

Proof for Theorem 5.99
uses 0

Apply the divergence theorem on the box to u grad v, expand div(u grad v), and rearrange the two integrals. Both summands are continuous on the compact box, so their Bochner integrability follows from the stated regularity.

Interchanging u and v in the first identity and subtracting removes the gradient term, since \nabla u\cdot\nabla v is symmetric. This requires C^2 regularity of both functions, whereas the first identity needs only C^1 for u.

Proof for Theorem 5.100
uses 1

Apply Green's first identity to (u,v) and (v,u), then subtract. Equivalently, apply the box divergence theorem directly to u grad v - v grad u; the mixed gradient terms cancel pointwise.

Uniqueness uses only the first identity, applied with u=v=w for the difference w of two solutions. Strictly positive side lengths give the box an interior on which continuity of \nabla w forces it to vanish pointwise.

Proof for Theorem 5.101
uses 1

Subtract the functions. Green's first identity and the zero face data force the Dirichlet energy to vanish. Continuity then makes every first derivative zero in the interior; convexity gives constancy, and the boundary value fixes that constant to zero.

5.4.1.2. Dirichlet's principle🔗

Green's first identity also explains why a solution of Poisson's equation minimizes an energy. For a bounded open set \Omega and a forcing f, put

I[w]=\int_\Omega\Bigl(\tfrac12|Dw|^2-fw\Bigr)\,dx.

If -\Delta u=f and w=u+v with v=0 on \partial\Omega, then

I[u+v]=I[u]+\int_\Omega(Du\cdot Dv-fv)\,dx+\frac12\int_\Omega|Dv|^2\,dx,

and integration by parts turns the middle term into \int_\Omega(-\Delta u-f)v\,dx=0. Conversely, a minimizer makes the first variation vanish in every compactly supported direction, and a continuous residual orthogonal to all test functions is zero. On a domain more general than a box, the integration by parts needs a boundary theory. The formal proof uses the zero-trace theorem on a domain with C^1 graph boundary and needs no C^2 extension of the domain or of the functions.

For \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n and f,g\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the classical energy of w is the integral I[w] above. The admissible class \mathcal A_g consists of the functions w that are C^2 on \Omega with derivatives through order two uniformly continuous there, continuous on \overline\Omega, and equal to g on \partial\Omega. The finite-energy class \mathcal A_g^f\subseteq\mathcal A_g consists of those w for which \frac12|Dw|^2-fw is integrable on \Omega.

Let n\ge1, let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be a bounded open set with C^1 graph boundary, let f be continuous on \Omega, and let u\in\mathcal A_g. Then

-\Delta u=f\ \text{in }\Omega \iff u\in\mathcal A_g^f\ \text{and}\ I[u]\le I[w]\ \text{for every } w\in\mathcal A_g^f.

If u\in\mathcal A_g^f minimizes I over \mathcal A_g^f, then \mathcal A_g^f=\mathcal A_g and u minimizes I over all of \mathcal A_g. When f is continuous on \overline\Omega, every member of \mathcal A_g has finite energy, and u solves -\Delta u=f exactly when I[u]\le I[w] for every w\in\mathcal A_g.

Proof for Theorem 5.103
uses 1

Suppose -\Delta u=f. The second derivatives of u are bounded on the bounded set \Omega, so f is square integrable there and every member of \mathcal A_g has finite energy. A competitor differs from u by a function v vanishing on \partial\Omega. On the C^1 graph domain such a v has zero trace and so lies in H^1_0(\Omega), which justifies the integration by parts in the expansion above; hence the competitor's energy is at least I[u].

Conversely, let u minimize over \mathcal A_g^f and let \varphi be smooth with compact support in \Omega. Interior continuity of f makes f\varphi integrable, so u+t\varphi stays in \mathcal A_g^f for every real t. The function t\mapsto I[u+t\varphi] is a quadratic polynomial with a minimum at t=0, and its derivative there is \int_\Omega(-\Delta u-f)\varphi\,dx. This vanishes for every \varphi, and the residual -\Delta u-f is continuous, so it is zero in \Omega.

For a finite-energy minimizer, f=-\Delta u in \Omega. The second derivatives of u are uniformly continuous there, so f agrees in \Omega with a continuous function on \mathbb R^n.

5.4.2. Weak Elliptic Problems🔗

5.4.2.1. Why Pass to a Weak Equation?🔗

There is a mismatch at the heart of elliptic theory. A classical solution of a second-order equation may need two pointwise derivatives, while the energy attached to that equation controls only one weak derivative. The weak formulation resolves it by moving a derivative onto a test function and asking for an identity in H^1_0(\Omega), which is exactly the level at which coercivity, compactness, and variational methods can build solutions.

5.4.2.2. Main Objects and Hypotheses🔗

An abstract weak problem is a bounded bilinear form a together with a bounded linear load F, and a solution satisfies

a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every test function }v.

The concrete Poisson solver assumes a bounded domain in positive dimension. Its Dirichlet form a is built from weak gradients; Poincaré's inequality promotes gradient control to coercivity on H^1_0. The solver is a bounded map of the square-integrable load, satisfies an a priori norm estimate, and is characterized by both the variational equation and minimization of the Dirichlet energy.

Variable principal coefficients enter first as bounded operators on the gradient coordinates, with pointwise L^\infty coefficient fields arriving through multiplication operators. Almost-everywhere uniform ellipticity gives an integrated lower bound by the Dirichlet form. Combining this bound with the bounded-domain Poincaré inequality gives the coercivity Lax–Milgram needs.

Lower-order terms can destroy positivity. What survives is a Gårding estimate, which says the form is coercive up to an L^2 error, and adding a large enough multiple of the pivot inner product turns that into a shifted coercive problem with a unique weak solution and a quantitative solver bound.

Almost-everywhere uniform ellipticity and integrated uniform ellipticity are different predicates: the first describes a coefficient field almost everywhere, the second is an integrated operator inequality, and passing from the first to the second is a theorem.

5.4.2.3. Weak Dirichlet Problems🔗

5.4.2.3.1. The variational route to Poisson's equation🔗

The weak theory begins with an abstract Hilbert-space equation

B(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v.

Lax–Milgram solves this equation when B is bounded and coercive. The Poisson problem is obtained by taking the Hilbert space to be H^1_0(\Omega), the bilinear form to be the Dirichlet energy pairing, and the load to be integration against f\in L^2(\Omega). Bounded-domain Poincaré control is the ingredient that upgrades gradient control to coercivity for the full Sobolev norm.

There are then two notions of solution. The variational equation tests against every element of H^1_0; the distributional equation tests against compactly supported smooth functions and reads as -\Delta u=f. Openness is needed only for the latter PDE-facing formulation. Density of smooth tests proves an equivalence, allowing existence and uniqueness to be proved abstractly and then transported to the distributional statement.

The final results explain the energy interpretation. Symmetry gives an exact completion of the square identity, so the weak solution is the minimizer of the Dirichlet functional. Coercivity makes that minimizer unique and also gives continuous dependence on the forcing datum.

For a bounded bilinear form B:H\times H\to\mathbb R and a continuous dual load \ell\in H^*, a weak solution is an element u\in H satisfying

B(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H.

This is Evans's variational definition for a bounded bilinear form B, which need not come from a differential operator.

Boundedness of B alone does not make the equation solvable, and the definition imposes no sign condition. The extra hypothesis is coercivity, a lower bound on the quadratic form B(v,v); symmetry of B is never required for existence and uniqueness, and it enters only in the energy interpretation below.

Proof for Theorem 5.105
uses 0

The load is transferred to its Riesz representative. Mathlib's Lax–Milgram continuous linear equivalence for the coercive form is then inverted, and injectivity of that equivalence gives uniqueness.

When B is symmetric, it is itself an inner product, equivalent to the one on H, and Lax–Milgram becomes the Riesz representation theorem in that inner product. The solution u is the minimizer of the energy J(v)=\frac12B(v,v)-\ell(v), whose level sets are the spheres of B centered at u. The left panel of the figure draws this in the plane, where B is a positive definite 2\times2 matrix and the spheres are ellipses. Restricting the equation to a closed subspace V_1 and solving B(u_1,v)=\ell(v) for v\in V_1 is again a Lax–Milgram problem, because coercivity passes to subspaces. Its solution u_1 is the point where a level ellipse touches the line, and subtracting the two equations gives B(u-u_1,v)=0 for every v\in V_1. So u_1 is the B-orthogonal projection of u, which is generally not the nearest point in the norm of H. Combining this orthogonality with boundedness and coercivity gives Céa's lemma, \lVert u-u_1\rVert\le(M/c)\inf_{v\in V_1}\lVert u-v\rVert. The Galerkin error is at most a fixed multiple of the best approximation error in the subspace. The right panels apply this to piecewise linear finite elements on nested meshes, where the best approximation error, and with it the Galerkin error, decays like the mesh size. Céa's lemma is the classical statement, checked numerically in the figure.

To reach Poisson's equation the abstract space is specialized to H^1_0(\Omega) and the form to the pairing of weak gradients. The form itself makes sense on any set; geometric restrictions on \Omega appear only when its lower bound is needed.

✓L∃∀N

On any set \Omega, the Dirichlet form on H^1_0(\Omega) is

B_\Omega(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^n \int_\Omega D_i u(x)\,D_i v(x)\,dx.

The derivatives are the canonical weak coordinate derivatives in the graph-space model of H^1_0(\Omega).

Lean code for Definition5.106●1 definition

    def SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.dirichletForm {n : ℕ} {Ω : Set ℝ^n} :
  SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.H10SpaceOn n Ω →L[ℝ]
    SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.H10SpaceOn n Ω →L[ℝ] ℝ
    def SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.dirichletForm
  {n : ℕ} {Ω : Set ℝ^n} :
  SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.H10SpaceOn n
      Ω →L[ℝ]
    SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.H10SpaceOn n
        Ω →L[ℝ]
      ℝ

    The Dirichlet energy bilinear form on H¹₀(Ω).

The quadratic form B_\Omega(u,u) is the squared L^2 norm of the weak gradient, so on its own it controls only the derivative coordinates of the graph-space norm. The base L^2 coordinate has to be recovered from the gradient, which is exactly what the Poincaré inequality does on a bounded domain.

Write that step in the usual Sobolev norm. If \|u\|_{L^2}\le C_P\|\nabla u\|_{L^2} for u\in H^1_0(\Omega), then

\|u\|_{H^1}^2 =\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2 \le(1+C_P^2)B_\Omega(u,u).

This is coercivity: small energy forces the whole state to be small in the solution norm. The zero boundary condition matters. Without it, adding an arbitrary constant leaves the gradient energy unchanged, so that energy cannot control the size of the function.

    Coercivity of the Dirichlet form on a bounded domain in every positive dimension.

Proof for Theorem 5.107
uses 0

The Dirichlet form is the squared L^2 norm of the weak gradient. On a bounded domain, Poincaré bounds the base L^2 norm of u by that gradient norm. Combining the two coordinates of the graph-space norm therefore yields a positive multiple controlled by B_\Omega(u,u).

With coercivity established, Lax–Milgram applies to B_\Omega and the load v\mapsto\int_\Omega fv for each f\in L^2(\Omega). Since that load depends linearly and continuously on f, the resulting assignment f\mapsto u is a bounded linear operator.

Proof for Theorem 5.109
uses 0

The solver is defined by applying the inverse Lax–Milgram equivalence to the L^2 load v\mapsto\int_\Omega fv. The defining inverse identity says precisely that its value satisfies the displayed weak equation for every test vector.

Up to this point the test functions have ranged over all of H^1_0(\Omega), and nothing about \Omega beyond measurability, boundedness, and positive dimension has been used. Reading the identity as the PDE -\Delta u=f means testing against \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega) instead, and compactly supported smooth test functions require \Omega to be open.

Let \Omega be any set, f\in L^2(\Omega), and u\in H^1_0(\Omega). The distributional Poisson predicate requires \Omega to be open and

\sum_{i=1}^n\int_\Omega D_i u\,D_i\varphi =\int_\Omega f\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).

This is the weak test form of -\Delta u=f.

Lean code for Definition5.110●1 definition

    complete

  (f : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.DerivLp n 2 Ω)
  (u : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.H10SpaceOn n Ω) : Prop
    def SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.IsWeakPoissonSolution
  {n : ℕ} {Ω : Set ℝ^n}
  (f :
    SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.DerivLp n 2 Ω)
  (u :
    SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.H10SpaceOn n
      Ω) :
  Prop

    The weak formulation of the homogeneous Dirichlet Poisson problem -Δu = f on an open set, tested against C_c^∞(Ω) as in Evans's identity (7) of §6.1.2.

    Openness is part of the proposition, rather than merely a theorem-side convention: on a positive-measure set with empty interior the class of compactly supported smooth test functions can be trivial, so the integral identity alone would not characterize a distributional PDE. Every displayed product is integrable: both weak derivatives and the forcing are in L², and the canonical test-function embedding places each test and its first derivatives in L². Thus the definition does not rely on the fallback value of Mathlib's totalized integral.

The two formulations differ only in the class of test functions. Since the canonical image of C_c^\infty(\Omega) is dense in H^1_0(\Omega) and both sides of the identity are continuous in the test function, restricting to smooth tests loses nothing; this equivalence needs openness of \Omega but neither boundedness nor positive dimension.

Proof for Theorem 5.111
uses 0

One implication evaluates the variational equation on the canonical image of each smooth test function. Conversely, equality on smooth tests extends to all of H^1_0(\Omega) because that image has dense range and both sides are continuous linear functionals.

Existence and uniqueness can therefore be transported from the variational side, where Lax–Milgram provides them, to the distributional side. The hypotheses are the union of those used so far: boundedness and positive dimension for coercivity, openness for the distributional predicate.

Theorem 5.105
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Construct the named Lax–Milgram solution for the coercive Dirichlet form and transport existence and uniqueness across the equivalence between the variational and smooth-test formulations.

Existence and uniqueness are two of the three components of well-posedness. The third, continuous dependence on the data, is for a linear problem a norm bound on the solution operator, and coercivity supplies it, since c_\Omega\lVert Sf\rVert^2\le B_\Omega(Sf,Sf)=\int_\Omega f\,Sf and the right-hand side is controlled by \lVert f\rVert_{L^2}\lVert Sf\rVert_{H^1_0}.

Proof for Theorem 5.113
uses 1

Apply the quantitative Lax–Milgram estimate with the coercivity constant, then bound the concrete L^2 load functional by the forcing norm.

Because S is linear, Sf-Sg=S(f-g), and the a priori estimate applied to the difference load turns the operator bound into a Lipschitz estimate. The zero-forcing identity S0=0 is the degenerate case of the same linearity.

Proof for Theorem 5.114
uses 1

Linearity identifies the difference of two solutions with the solution of the difference load. Apply the Lax–Milgram operator bound and then the norm bound for the concrete L^2 load functional.

The Dirichlet form is also symmetric, and symmetry allows the weak equation to be recast as the stationarity condition of a quadratic functional.

Proof for Theorem 5.116
uses 0

Expand both quadratic terms, use symmetry of the Dirichlet form, and replace B(u,v) and B(u,u) by the load functional through the weak equation.

The right-hand side of the identity is nonnegative, since B_\Omega(w,w)=\sum_i\lVert D_iw\rVert_{L^2}^2. Minimality of the named solution therefore follows from the identity alone; boundedness of \Omega enters only through the existence of Sf, not through the inequality.

Theorem 5.109
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Apply the energy identity at the named weak solution. The remaining Dirichlet quadratic form is a sum of squared L^2 derivative norms and is therefore nonnegative.

Uniqueness of the minimizer is where coercivity, and not merely nonnegativity, is needed. Equality J(v)=J(u) forces B_\Omega(v-u,v-u)=0, and only the Poincaré lower bound converts vanishing Dirichlet energy into v=u. Conversely, every minimizer agrees with the named weak solution and therefore satisfies its weak equation.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

On a bounded domain of positive dimension, coercivity gives

J(v)-J(u)=\frac12B(v-u,v-u)\ge0,

with equality exactly when v=u. Thus the named weak solution is the unique minimizer of the Dirichlet functional. More generally, minimizing J is equivalent to the weak Euler–Lagrange equation B(u,w)=\ell(w) for every test direction w.

The completion of the square identity reduces equality of energies to vanishing Dirichlet energy of the difference. Poincaré coercivity forces that difference to be zero, and the weak equation identifies the minimizer in both directions.

5.4.2.4. Principal Divergence-Form Problems🔗

5.4.2.4.1. Principal forms and ellipticity🔗

The principal divergence-form equation replaces the identity matrix in Poisson's equation by a coefficient field:

-D_i\!\left(a^{ij}D_j u\right)=f.

We first represent the coefficients as a finite matrix of bounded operators on L^2(\Omega). Pointwise multiplication by an L^\infty matrix field recovers the local PDE model, while the operator-valued form is also meaningful for bounded nonlocal coefficients.

Almost-everywhere pointwise ellipticity of the matrix field is integrated against the weak gradient. That produces coercivity of the principal form after Poincaré controls the L^2 coordinate. Lax–Milgram then constructs the unique element of H^1_0(\Omega), and the smooth-test bridge identifies its variational equation with the displayed divergence-form PDE.

Each hypothesis has one job: measurability and essential boundedness define the multiplication operators, ellipticity controls the gradient, boundedness of the domain supplies Poincaré, and openness supplies compactly supported smooth test functions.

    For multiplication operators induced by a measurable matrix field, the usual pointwise condition xiᵀ A(x) xi ≥ alpha |xi|² almost everywhere implies this predicate by integration.

The pointwise ellipticity hypothesis constrains the matrix a(x) for almost every x and every direction \xi. It only makes sense for multiplication operators, which is why it is a separate definition rather than a special case of the integrated one.

uses 0used by 1✓L∃∀N

For a measurable L^\infty matrix field a, Evans's pointwise condition requires a single \alpha>0 such that, for almost every x and every \xi\in\mathbb R^n, one has

\alpha |\xi|^2\le \sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x)\xi_j\xi_i.

The matrix need not be symmetric: only its symmetric part contributes to this quadratic inequality, and the coercivity result below applies to nonsymmetric coefficients satisfying the same condition.

The two notions are compatible in the expected direction. Choosing \xi=\nabla u(x) in the pointwise inequality and integrating over \Omega recovers the integrated inequality for the multiplication realization, with the same constant \alpha.

Proof for Theorem 5.122
uses 0

Apply the pointwise matrix inequality to the measurable vector of weak derivatives and integrate. Hölder integrability of each coefficient-gradient product justifies the finite sums and integrals.

The integrated hypothesis feeds the Hilbert-space theory, while the PDE reading of the problem needs the concrete L^\infty coefficients and compactly supported smooth tests. As for Poisson's equation, the distributional predicate carries the openness of \Omega with it.

For an open measurable domain, a^{ij}\in L^\infty(\Omega), f\in L^2(\Omega), and u\in H^1_0(\Omega), the weak-solution predicate stores the openness of \Omega and records

\sum_{i,j=1}^n\int_\Omega a^{ij}(x)D_j u(x)D_i\varphi(x)\,dx =\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx

for every \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega). This is the concrete distributional equation for -D_i(a^{ij}D_j u)=f. A separate density theorem identifies it with the operator-valued variational identity tested against every v\in H^1_0(\Omega).

Let A=(A_{ij}) be a matrix of bounded operators on L^2(\Omega). On a bounded measurable domain in positive dimension, suppose A is integrated-uniformly elliptic: for some \alpha>0,

\alpha B_\Omega(u,u)\le B_A(u,u) \qquad\text{for every }u\in H^1_0(\Omega).

Then the variable-coefficient form satisfies B_A(u,u)\ge c\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}^2 for some c>0. For a pointwise L^\infty coefficient matrix, the preceding almost-everywhere-to-integrated theorem supplies this hypothesis from Evans's pointwise ellipticity condition.

Represent the coefficient field by its bounded multiplication operators, deduce coercivity from almost-everywhere ellipticity, apply Lax–Milgram, and translate the Hilbert-space equation back to the concrete weak integral identity.

5.4.2.5. Lower-Order Divergence-Form Problems🔗

5.4.2.5.1. Lower-order terms and coercive shifts🔗

First- and zeroth-order terms need not preserve coercivity, even when the principal coefficient matrix is uniformly elliptic. The replacement is a Gårding inequality: the full form controls the gradient up to a multiple of the L^2 norm. Adding a sufficiently large positive mass term absorbs that loss and restores a coercive problem. This is the content of Gårding's inequality (1953), which Evans (2010, pp. 318–319) states for L^\infty coefficients and Brezis (2011) (Proposition 9.22) places in the functional-analytic framework of compact perturbations of coercive operators.

We make the threshold explicit. Bounds for the first-order operators are combined with Young's inequality, the zeroth-order operator is controlled by its norm, and the resulting constants determine the coercive shift. Every larger shift gives the same uniform coercivity lower bound and therefore a unique Lax–Milgram solution.

The forcing is written in the standard H^{-1} form f_0-\sum_iD_i f^i. In Lean this is a continuous functional assembled from one base L^2 component and one component for each weak derivative.

A one-dimensional model shows why a shift can be needed. Let L>0. On \Omega=(0,L), consider the operator -u''-cu=f in weak form:

B_c(u,v)=\int_0^L u'v'\,dx-c\int_0^L uv\,dx.

Take \phi(x)=\sin(\pi x/L), the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of -d^2/dx^2 on (0,L) with eigenvalue \lambda_1=(\pi/L)^2. Then

B_c(\phi,\phi)=\lambda_1\lVert\phi\rVert_2^2-c\lVert\phi\rVert_2^2 =(\lambda_1-c)\lVert\phi\rVert_2^2.

When c<\lambda_1, the form is positive on every eigenspace and hence coercive on all of H^1_0(0,L). When c=\lambda_1, the form vanishes on the one-dimensional eigenspace of \phi; coercivity fails, and the equation -u''-\lambda_1 u=f has no solution unless f\perp\phi (the Fredholm alternative). When c>\lambda_1, the form is negative on that eigenspace.

Adding the mass shift \mu\int_0^L uv replaces B_c by

B_c^\mu(u,v)=\int_0^L u'v'-c\int_0^L uv+\mu\int_0^L uv =\int_0^L u'v'+(\mu-c)\int_0^L uv.

On the eigenspace of \phi, B_c^\mu(\phi,\phi)=(\lambda_1-c+\mu)\lVert\phi\rVert_2^2. Thus any \mu>c-\lambda_1 restores positivity in this eigendirection, and since higher eigenvalues are larger, coercivity holds on all of H^1_0. The general Gårding estimate below performs the same correction without diagonalizing the operator. It uses only Young's inequality and the coefficient bounds to find an explicit \mu_0 that works uniformly (Evans, 2010, pp. 318–319; Gilbarg and Trudinger (2001), Section 8.1).

Lower-order terms also change what should count as forcing. The natural dual of H^1_0(\Omega) is H^{-1}(\Omega), whose elements need not be functions, so the loads are allowed to contain first derivatives of L^2 functions from the start.

uses 0

Extend the functional isometrically to the ambient base-gradient product, take its Riesz representative, and read the base and first-derivative coordinates as f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_n. The product-space norm decomposition gives the squared-norm identity.

The predicate below combines the full form, the generalized load, and a mass shift \mu into one distributional equation. The shift is the parameter that will be adjusted to restore coercivity; \mu=0 is the original unshifted problem, whose solvability is the Fredholm question.

For a measurable domain, L^\infty coefficients a, b, and c, a shift \mu, standard H^{-1} data (f_0,f^1,\ldots,f^n), and u\in H^1_0(\Omega), the predicate requires \Omega to be open and records

If the principal form has ellipticity constant \alpha>0, the constants \beta,\gamma are nonnegative, each first-order operator has norm at most \beta, and the zeroth-order operator has norm at most \gamma, then

\frac{\alpha}{2}B_0(u,u) \le B(u,u)+\left(\frac{n\beta^2}{2\alpha}+\gamma\right) \lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2.

Here B_0(u,u)=\sum_i\lVert D_i u\rVert_2^2 is the Dirichlet form. This is Gårding's estimate (Evans, 2010, pp. 318–319) for operator-valued coefficients.

Proof for Theorem 5.130
uses 0

Bound each first-order pairing by Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality, sum over coordinates, bound the zeroth-order pairing by its operator norm, and combine the result with principal ellipticity.

Read with the mass term moved to the left, Gårding's inequality says that B(u,u)+\mu\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2 dominates (\alpha/2)B_0(u,u) together with \bigl(\mu-\tfrac{n\beta^2}{2\alpha}-\gamma\bigr)\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2. Choosing the shift so that the second coefficient equals \alpha/2 makes both graph-space coordinates appear with the same constant.

Proof for Theorem 5.132
uses 0

Add the mass shift to Gårding's inequality, decompose the graph-space norm into its L^2 and gradient components, and use monotonicity in \mu.

Coercivity of the shifted form is exactly the hypothesis of Lax–Milgram, so the shifted problem is uniquely solvable for every generalized load. For pointwise L^\infty coefficients the operator bounds \beta,\gamma are the L^\infty norms of b^i and c, and boundedness of \Omega is not required, in contrast with the unshifted principal problem.

The Gårding estimate at the explicit threshold is strengthened by the nonnegative extra mass term when \mu is larger. Lax–Milgram then gives the unique Hilbert-space solution, and the smooth-test density bridge identifies it with the concrete shifted divergence-form weak equation.

Uniqueness makes the solution a function of the data, and at the canonical shift \mu_0 that function can be named. The definition lives at the operator-valued level, where only integrated ellipticity and the operator-norm bounds are available.

uses 0

Proof for Theorem 5.136
uses 0

Test the solver equation with v=u. Coercivity at the canonical shift gives (\alpha/2)\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}^2 on the left, while Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the generalized load by (\lVert f_0\rVert_2+\sum_i\lVert f^i\rVert_2) \lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}. Cancel the solution norm to obtain the displayed factor 2/\alpha.

For local L^\infty multiplication coefficients the shifted problem also satisfies weak comparison (weak comparison). Under the integrated ellipticity and lower-order bounds above, fix the same coefficients and shift \mu\geq\mu_0 for two weak solutions u,v\in H^1_0(\Omega). If their dual loads obey \ell_1(t)\leq\ell_2(t) for every almost-everywhere nonnegative t\in H^1_0(\Omega), then u\leq v almost everywhere on \Omega.

Test the difference equation with w=(u-v)^+. The supported Sobolev closure is preserved by this operation, and D_iw=\mathbf{1}_{\{u>v\}}D_i(u-v) almost everywhere, including on \{u=v\}. Local multiplication then gives B_\mu(u-v,w)=B_\mu(w,w). Load order makes this quantity nonpositive; coercivity forces w=0. This localization is why comparison uses multiplication coefficients even though the solver permits nonlocal operators.

At the canonical shift, the scalar-load comparison theorem specializes this argument to ordered scalar L^2 loads with the divergence forcing held fixed. Comparison needs only measurable \Omega: here the zero-boundary space means the closure of supported smooth functions. On open domains this is the usual H^1_0(\Omega). Neither boundedness nor a boundary atlas is required; the conclusion is an almost-everywhere inequality between weak solutions.

Comparison also gives a route to a nonlinear equation. Let \Omega now be bounded and measurable, and suppose ordered weak lower and upper solutions \underline u,\overline u\in H^1_0(\Omega) are given for Lu=g(u). Suppose g is continuous, has at most linear growth, and s\mapsto g(s)+Ms is increasing for some real M. Choose \mu=\max\{\mu_0,M\}. The shifted reaction s\mapsto g(s)+\mu s is then increasing, so the map

T(w)=(L+\mu)^{-1}\bigl(g(w)+\mu w\bigr)

preserves order. Weak comparison and the barrier inequalities give \underline u\leq T(\underline u) and T(\overline u)\leq\overline u. Starting at the lower barrier produces

\underline u=u_0\leq u_1\leq u_2\leq\cdots\leq\overline u, \qquad u_{k+1}=T(u_k).

The barriers bound this sequence in L^2, and the linear growth estimate bounds the shifted loads there. The linear solver bounds the iterates in H^1_0; Rellich compactness then supplies an L^2 limit. Monotonicity makes the whole sequence converge, and continuity of the solver also gives convergence in H^1_0. At the fixed point the two mass terms cancel, leaving Lu=g(u).

The monotone iteration theorem carries out this construction with the same rough multiplication coefficients as comparison. Consider g(s)=1+\sqrt{\max\{s,0\}}. It is increasing, so we can take M=0; the estimate |g(s)|\leq 2+|s| supplies linear growth. Its slope becomes unbounded near zero, but continuity is enough to pass to the limit in L^2. Zero is a lower barrier, and any nonnegative weak upper barrier encloses a solution. Globally Lipschitz reactions, including g(s)=1+|s|, are special cases with M equal to the Lipschitz constant.

Often the barriers give a bounded range [a,b] for every iterate. Then we only need continuity of g and monotonicity of g(s)+Ms on that interval. Let P(s)=\min\{\max\{s,a\},b\} and extend the reaction by

\widetilde g(s)=g(P(s))+M P(s)-Ms.

On [a,b] this is exactly g. The shifted function \widetilde g(s)+Ms is increasing and bounded, so \widetilde g has linear growth on the whole line. The preceding construction applies, and the barriers keep its solution where the extension agrees with g. The interval-reaction existence theorem formalizes this argument. For instance, it handles 1+s^3 on [0,R] without a global growth bound for the cubic. Both barriers belong to the zero-boundary space throughout this construction.

5.4.2.5.2. From signed-trace barriers to a classical solution🔗

For smooth coefficients and boundary, the barriers can instead lie in H^1(\Omega): their traces need only bracket the prescribed zero boundary value. The solution still belongs to H^1_0(\Omega). Keeping its values between fixed constants makes local smoothness of the reaction sufficient for the regularity argument.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with smooth boundary. Suppose the coefficients a^{ij},b^i,c are smooth up to the boundary and a is uniformly elliptic. Let f be smooth on an open neighborhood of [\ell,r]. Assume ordered weak barriers \underline u,\overline u\in H^1(\Omega) satisfy

\ell\leq\underline u\leq\overline u\leq r \quad\text{almost everywhere},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\underline u\leq0\leq\operatorname{Tr}\overline u \quad\text{surface-almost everywhere},

and the subsolution and supersolution inequalities for every nonnegative H^1_0 test function, using the full divergence-form operator below. Then there are u\in H^1_0(\Omega) and a representative z=u almost everywhere, smooth on \overline\Omega, such that

-\sum_{i,j}\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_jz) +\sum_i b^i\partial_i z+cz=f(z)\quad\text{in }\Omega, \qquad z=0\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.

The representative lies in [\ell,r] at every interior point and between the two Sobolev barriers almost everywhere. The principal matrix need not be symmetric, and the potential need not have a fixed sign.

    Smooth geometry and coefficients, and a reaction smooth near the bounded barrier range, give a classical zero-boundary solution between ordered H¹ subsolutions and supersolutions with signed traces. No regularity of a sought solution is assumed. The result holds in every positive spatial dimension.

Proof for Theorem 5.137
uses 0

The signed-trace comparison argument constructs a weak zero-boundary solution between the barriers. Its bounded range controls the derivatives of the reaction needed at each stage of Sobolev composition. Global elliptic regularity then bootstraps the solution through every finite Sobolev order. Morrey regularity supplies one smooth representative on the closure. The trace-kernel identity makes that representative zero at every boundary point. Finally, the weak equation gives the full divergence-form identity almost everywhere; continuity promotes it to a pointwise equation in the interior.

5.4.3. Modified Helmholtz Equation🔗

5.4.3.1. The role of the positive mass term🔗

The homogeneous-Dirichlet modified Helmholtz problem is

-\Delta u+\lambda u=f,\qquad u\in H^1_0(\Omega).

Its weak form pairs gradients and adds the mass term \lambda\int_\Omega uv. When \lambda>0, the two terms directly control the full graph-space norm: the gradient controls the derivative coordinates and the mass term controls the base L^2 coordinate. This is why coercivity holds without boundedness of the domain or a Poincaré inequality.

There are two levels. On an arbitrary set, the bilinear form and its Lax–Milgram solver are functional-analytic objects. On an open set, compactly supported smooth functions are available as PDE test functions, so the same solution can be read distributionally. Density of those tests in H^1_0 makes the two formulations equivalent.

Besides positive \lambda, we treat a signed regime, in which a negative mass contribution is allowed whenever its size is smaller than an available Dirichlet coercivity modulus.

For \lambda>0, on every set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n and in every dimension, the form B_\lambda is coercive on H^1_0(\Omega): there is a constant c>0 with

B_\lambda(u,u)\ge c\,\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2 \qquad\text{for all } u\in H^1_0(\Omega).

    For λ > 0, the modified Helmholtz form is coercive with constant min 1 λ.

    Unlike the pure Dirichlet form, this proof uses the positive mass term to control the base coordinate. Consequently it applies on every measurable domain and in every dimension.

Proof for Theorem 5.139
uses 0

Expanding B_\lambda(u,u) gives the squared gradient norm plus \lambda times the squared base L^2 norm. Each coefficient is bounded below by \min(1,\lambda)>0, so their sum controls that constant times the full graph-space norm squared; c=\min(1,\lambda) is the constant the proof supplies.

When \lambda is negative the mass term works against coercivity, and a lower bound can only come from the gradient term, through a Dirichlet coercivity modulus. On bounded domains of positive dimension, Poincaré's inequality supplies one.

Suppose the Dirichlet form has a coercivity modulus c:

c\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2 \leq\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2 \qquad(u\in H^1_0(\Omega)).

If the negative part of the mass coefficient satisfies \lambda^-<c, then

B_\lambda(u,u)\geq (c-\lambda^-)\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0(\Omega)}^2.

Proof for Theorem 5.140
uses 0

Write \lambda=\lambda^+-\lambda^-. The positive part can be discarded. The base-coordinate norm is bounded by the full graph-space norm, so the negative mass contribution is bounded below by -\lambda^-\lVert u\rVert_{H^1_0}^2. Subtracting this from the Dirichlet lower bound leaves the positive coefficient c-\lambda^-.

The signed result gives coercivity, hence unique solvability through Lax–Milgram. The named solver, and every result built on it, is stated for \lambda>0. It is the Lax–Milgram solution for the L^2 load v\mapsto\int_\Omega fv.

On every domain and for \lambda>0, the solver sends zero data to zero. Moreover, there is a constant C>0, depending on the fixed form, such that for all f,g\in L^2(\Omega),

\lVert S_\lambda f\rVert_{H^1_0} \leq C\lVert f\rVert_{L^2}, \qquad \lVert S_\lambda f-S_\lambda g\rVert_{H^1_0} \leq C\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2}.

Proof for Theorem 5.142
uses 0

The zero-data identity follows from uniqueness. Boundedness of the Lax–Milgram solution operator gives the first estimate for some positive constant depending only on the fixed form. Apply the same estimate to f-g and use linearity of the solver to obtain the Lipschitz bound.

The form B_\lambda is symmetric, so the weak equation admits a variational characterization. The functional is the Dirichlet functional with the mass term added to its quadratic part.

If \lambda\geq0, every weak solution minimizes J_{\lambda,f}. If \lambda>0, coercivity makes the characterization exact:

u\text{ is a global minimizer of }J_{\lambda,f} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_\lambda(u,v)=\int_\Omega fv\quad(\forall v\in H^1_0(\Omega)).

The named solution S_\lambda f is the unique minimizer, and every other field has strictly larger energy.

Proof for Theorem 5.144
uses 0

Symmetry and nonnegativity expand the energy difference around a weak solution into one half of B_\lambda(v-u,v-u). For nonnegative \lambda this proves minimality. For positive \lambda, coercivity makes the difference vanish only when v=u, giving the converse, strictness, and uniqueness.

Everything so far has been Hilbert-space theory on an arbitrary set. To read B_\lambda(u,v)=\int_\Omega fv as the PDE -\Delta u+\lambda u=f, assume \Omega is open and test against compactly supported smooth functions. The raw smooth-test identity makes sense on arbitrary sets; the solution predicate requires openness.

    The distributional weak formulation of the homogeneous-Dirichlet modified Helmholtz problem -Δu + λu = f on an open domain, tested against compactly supported smooth functions as in Evans's (7) of §6.1.2.

    Fields

    isOpen : IsOpen Ω

    The PDE domain is open.

    equation : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.ModifiedHelmholtzTestIdentity lam f u

    The modified Helmholtz identity against every compactly supported smooth test.

The variational and distributional formulations differ only in their test classes, and the canonical image of C_c^\infty(\Omega) is dense in H^1_0(\Omega). The equivalence therefore holds for every real \lambda, coercive or not; the sign of \lambda matters only for solvability.

Proof for Theorem 5.146
uses 0

One direction evaluates the Hilbert-space identity on canonical smooth tests. For the reverse direction, density of smooth compactly supported tests in H^1_0 and continuity of both sides extend equality to every Sobolev test.

Combining the equivalence with the coercive Lax–Milgram theory transports existence and uniqueness to the distributional side.

Theorem 5.105
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Construct the coercive Lax–Milgram solution, transfer its weak equation to the distributional predicate, and use the same equivalence plus uniqueness of the coercive Hilbert-space problem for any competing solution.

Uniqueness can be sharpened to an identification: any distributional solution must coincide with the named solver. This is the form in which the result is most useful, since it converts statements about the PDE into statements about a single operator.

The distributional equivalence turns the PDE predicate into the variational weak equation. The solver characterization and uniqueness of the coercive problem then identify u with S_\lambda f. For zero forcing, combine this equivalence with the solver's zero-data identity.

Linearity of the distributional predicate in the pair (f,u) holds for every real \lambda, since it is a property of the integral identity alone. Through the identification with the named solver it becomes linearity of S_\lambda for \lambda>0.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

Distributional modified Helmholtz solutions are closed under addition, negation, subtraction, and real scalar multiplication, with the forcing data transformed by the same operation. Consequently, for \lambda>0,

S_\lambda(f+g)=S_\lambda f+S_\lambda g, \qquad S_\lambda(c f)=cS_\lambda f.

Proof for Theorem 5.149
uses 0

Linearity of the integral and gradient identities proves closure of the distributional predicate under the listed operations. When \lambda>0, the characterization by the unique named solver turns those closure results into the two displayed solver identities.
